name: Multi-tenant SaaS analytics
description: A SaaS product serving analytics back to its customers needs one pipeline and many audiences: product data replicates into an analytics store where every table is tenant-keyed, an isolation layer guarantees each customer sees only their rows — via row-level security, per-tenant schemas, or per-tenant databases — and dashboards embed into the product behind that boundary. The design axis is the isolation model: pooled tables with RLS are cheap and scale to thousands of tenants; schema-per-tenant eases compliance and noisy-neighbor control; database-per-tenant maximizes isolation at maximum operational cost. Most platforms mix models by customer tier.
when_to_use: Customer-facing analytics is a product feature: every tenant needs dashboards over their own slice of the same schema.
Tenant counts are large enough that per-customer manual BI provisioning cannot scale.
Enterprise tiers demand stronger isolation or residency guarantees than the pooled tier provides — the model must support mixing.
Usage-based pricing or plan limits require per-tenant metering of analytics workloads.
when_not_to_use: Analytics is internal-only — ordinary warehouse layering (2, 26) with standard embedded dashboards (22) is enough.
There are a handful of large customers — dedicated per-customer stacks may be simpler than a generic isolation layer.
Dashboard latency demands are sub-second at high concurrency and the warehouse can't serve it — add a real-time OLAP store (8) behind the same isolation layer.
The product has no analytics surface yet — validate demand with simple exports before building tenancy machinery.

hot_spots.title: Tenant leakage
hot_spots.detail: One missing tenant filter in one query path exposes another customer's data — the single worst incident this architecture can produce.

hot_spots.title: Noisy neighbors
hot_spots.detail: One large tenant's queries starve everyone else's dashboards unless workload isolation and quotas are designed in.

hot_spots.title: Schema sprawl
hot_spots.detail: Per-tenant schemas multiply every migration by the tenant count; at thousands of tenants, deploys become the bottleneck.

hot_spots.title: Cost attribution
hot_spots.detail: Without per-tenant metering you cannot price plans, cap abuse, or explain why the warehouse bill doubled.

stages.name: Product database
stages.rationale: Whatever the product runs on — the analytics stack's job is to replicate from it without adding load.

stages.name: Replication
stages.role: Continuous, low-impact copy of tenant data into the analytics store
stages.rationale: CDC keeps tenant dashboards minutes-fresh without hammering the product database; managed EL works when hourly freshness is acceptable.

stages.name: Analytics store
stages.role: Tenant-keyed analytical tables with native isolation primitives
stages.rationale: ClickHouse row policies plus high-concurrency, low-latency reads fit customer-facing dashboards; Snowflake row access policies and BigQuery authorized views are the managed equivalents.

stages.name: Isolation + semantic API
stages.role: The layer that injects tenant context and guarantees scoped queries
stages.rationale: Cube's security context binds every query to the signed tenant claim and adds caching — enforcing isolation in one place instead of every dashboard.

stages.name: Embedded analytics
stages.role: Dashboards rendered inside the product behind the tenant boundary
stages.rationale: Superset and Metabase embed cheaply at scale; Power BI Embedded and Looker fit when buyers expect a commercial BI experience.

stages.name: Metering + cost attribution
stages.role: Per-tenant usage tracking for pricing, quotas, and cost control
stages.rationale: Query logs tagged with tenant context feed dashboards that price plans and catch noisy neighbors before other tenants notice.
